summary: Technical deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategy. Covered hit rate tradeoffs, cache key design, multi-tenant isolation, eviction & TTL, KV cache internals, batching interactions, quantization impacts, and VPC/on-prem considerations. Agreed to run benchmarks with Zenith prompt set, prototype tenant-isolated caching config, and share security artifacts. Next: pilot kickoff scheduling.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick roll call, uh Alex Chen here from Redwood, with Priya our systems SE.
[00:12] Priya: hi all, excited to dig in.
[00:15] Jordan: Jordan Lee, Zenith. we want to focus on prefix caching, hit rates, how this plays with our multi-tenant stack.
[00:23] Maya: Maya Rivera, ML eng, i'll be sending prompt samples later.
[00:26] Sam: Sam Patel, infra. i'm mostly concerned with VPC and isolation.
[00:30] Alex: great. Agenda is quick architecture, then hit rates and cache keys, then safety/tenant isolation, eviction/ttl, batching implications, and finally on-prem / VPC notes. sound good?
[00:39] Jordan: yep.
[00:40] Priya: ok i'll start with a quick overview of how Redwood's prefix cache works in hosted and dedicated modes. bear with me, i'll keep it high level first then we'll go deeper.
[00:49] Priya: so conceptually we store KV entries for prefixes — conversation or prompt prefix tokens — the value is the KV cache blob (attention + layerstates) which lets us avoid recomputing early layers for repeated prompts. it's implemented as an in-memory LRU with optional backing on nvme for warmup and for Dedicated we can pin to faster tiers. we call it pre-fix cache internally, sometimes prefex, so apologies for the mispronunciation.
[01:15] Maya: quick q: is the cache per-model or per-model-version?
[01:19] Priya: per model checkpoint + quantization profile + sequence length bucket. keys encode model id and quantization tag, so different quantized variants don't collide. for multi-tenant we either namespace keys by tenant id or use separate cache instances depending on deployment.
[01:34] Sam: separate instances for tenants — that sounds heavy. what's the memory overhead?
[01:37] Priya: yes it's heavier. tradeoffs: separate instances give strong isolation (no accidental data leakage), but you pay memory headroom. our Dedicated offering often uses tenant pools where several related tenants share a pool; on-prem / VPC can be single-tenant. for hosted we usually namespace keys with a tenant prefix and enforce RBAC + encryption.
[01:56] Jordan: what's the risk of stale or wrong cache hits across tenants if we just namespace?
[02:02] Priya: if you namespace correctly there is virtually zero risk of cross-tenant collision — the collision vector is key design. but mis-keys or poor fingerprinting can cause false positives. so best practice: include tenant id, model id, model-sha, quantization tag, and explicit prompt fingerprint. we also include prefix-length bucketing (like first 64/128 tokens) as part of keys.
[02:23] Alex: to add, we also sign keys and run integrity checks — when security mode is strict we verify key signatures and reject cache hits that fail integrity.
[02:33] Maya: how do you fingerprint prompts? hashing?
[02:36] Priya: yes we use SHA-256 over normalized prompt text plus any fixed system instructions and meta fields; normalization includes whitespace collapsing, canonicalizing quotes, and substituting user-specific tokens for placeholders. but hashing alone isn't enough — we also store a short token-prob distribution checksum to catch model-side mismatches.
[02:55] Sam: what about evictions and TTLs — we have highly dynamic queries, some stale prefixes might be reused later.
[03:02] Priya: we support per-key TTLs and an LRU eviction. typical defaults: 1 hour TTL for chat prefix caching in high-throughput flows, 24 hours for relatively static system prompts. But that's a starting point — empirical tuning is needed. Hit rate is the key metric: if hit rate < 10% we're wasting memory and complexity. we recommend running a week-long sampling to compute prefix re-use distribution.
[03:27] Jordan: do you have instrumentation exposed?
[03:30] Alex: yes, Redwood console shows per-route cache hit rate, average saved tokens, average latency delta, and per-model KV cache size. we'll share the dashboard screenshots and the CSV export.
[03:40] Maya: ok, can you walk through hit-rate math — what's a realistic improvement for us?
[03:44] Priya: ballpark: for customer with lots of templated prompts we see 30-60% early-layer savings, translating to 20-40% lower tail latency and 15-35% compute reduction. worst case (highly unique prompts) it's near zero. It depends heavily on prompt templating and canonicalization.
[04:05] Jordan: what about batching — if we cache prefixes, does that reduce batching efficiency?
[04:09] Priya: good question. caching reduces per-token compute but can increase variability in per-request compute time, which affects packing. our runtime supports dynamic batching and shards by similar sequence lengths and cached status. we have a scheduler that tries to batch cached & uncached requests separately to avoid head-of-line blocking. in practice, we maintain throughput but see improved average latency when cache hit rates are decent.
[04:34] Sam: are cached entries compatible across different quantization levels?
[04:36] Priya: no — cache entries are quantization-specific. we tag entries by quantization profile (e.g., q4_0 vs q8_0) because kernel paths and layer outputs differ. using the wrong variant would yield silent correctness errors.
[04:50] Jordan: ok that makes sense. on security, we need to make sure no PII leaks through cache. if one tenant has a conversation and another request matches a prefix hash, namespace prevents cross-tenant hits, but is there any risk of de-anonymization?
[05:04] Priya: main risks are improper key derivation or shared backing stores without encryption. mitigations: tenant namespaces, encrypt-on-disk with per-tenant keys (KMS/HSM), and access controls. for Dedicated and Private we offer per-tenant KMS integration. for hosted we use envelope encryption per-tenant and strict audit logs.
[05:24] Maya: can we rotate keys without invalidating large parts of the cache?
[05:27] Alex: we support key rotation with versioned encryption keys; when rotating, we keep old keys for decrypting existing entries for a grace period and re-encrypt on write, so cold start is gradual. you can also opt to evict on rotate if you want immediate cleansing.
[05:43] Jordan: what about on-prem / VPC deployment constraints — we want to run Redwood private in our VPC, do you run a separate cache instance or integrate with our memcached/redis?
[05:53] Priya: we have two patterns: 1) Redwood-managed in-cluster cache that lives alongside the runtime (recommended for performance) or 2) integrate with your existing Redis cluster using a strict key schema. pattern 1 gives best latency since it's in-process or local-nvme backed; pattern 2 is easier for operations but adds network hop and potential cross-tenant hazards if Redis isn't properly namespaced and secured.
[06:16] Sam: latency numbers?
[06:18] Priya: local in-memory KV hit adds ~0.2-0.6 ms; NVMe-backed warm read ~1-3ms; uncached compute for first prefix layer could be 20-60ms depending on model size and quantization. these are roughs — depends on GPU packing and sequence length.
[06:33] Maya: quantization interplay again — does quantization increase or decrease the benefit of prefix caching?
[06:37] Priya: quantization reduces nv compute cost and memory pressure, so uncached forward is cheaper; however prefix caching still helps because early-layer activations are independent of quantization benefits. for very small models the relative win is smaller. for large models (7B+) caching can cut a lot of repeated computation.
[06:55] Jordan: any gotchas with adaptive caching for conversational flows where user edits earlier history?
[07:00] Priya: yes — if the prefix changes (user edits, insertion), your stored prefix becomes invalid. our approach: store multiple prefix granularities and detection heuristics. we also support diff-aware invalidation where backend recomputes only the affected layers if edit offset small. that's more complex and heavier in instrumentation.
[07:20] Alex: to be explicit — key design includes prefix-text-hash, canonicalized system instructions, tenant id, model id, quant tag, and sequence-length-bucket. hashing collisions are improbable with SHA256 but we also store a short plaintext snippet (first 64 chars) to help debug false-positives.
[07:39] Sam: debugging tools? how do we surface false hits or metrics?
[07:42] Priya: ops dashboard includes per-route hit/miss traces, sample cache keys, and a peek at the stored prefix snippet (redacted in strict mode). we can also emit traces into your tracing system via OTLP so you can correlate.
[07:58] Maya: let's talk numbers for our workload. we have templated outputs: ~60% of queries are templated, average prefix length 80 tokens, typical user tokens 30. what hit rate should we expect?
[08:10] Priya: with templated prompts that are canonicalized well, i'd expect 40-55% hit rate on prefix-level for first-pass caching; effective compute saving depends on how much of compute is in prefix (for you seems significant). running real benchmarks will give a definite number — we'll run with your 500 sample templates and report back.
[08:29] Jordan: benchmark plan?
[08:30] Alex: we'll run three workload profiles: low (50 rps), med (200 rps), high (1k rps) with your sample prompts and measure hit rate, avg latency p50/p95, tokens saved, and cost delta. we'll also vary TTLs (5m, 1h, 24h) and show tradeoffs. Priya will run dedicated-style config and hosted-style config.
[08:48] Priya: also we'll include a scenario where we enable tenant-isolation (separate cache instance) vs namespaced keys to show memory overhead and hit rates.
[08:57] Sam: for VPC/private we need to ensure the cache process doesn't have external network access, is that typical?
[09:02] Priya: yes for Private deployments the cache processes can be confined to your private subnets with no outbound internet. we support KMS connectors that are either customer-hosted HSM or a proxy in your network.
[09:14] Maya: regression testing — if we change model version, how do you handle cache invalidation?
[09:18] Priya: model version is part of the key; rolling model changes won't hit old cache entries. for canary rollouts we recommend model-id tagging and a fallback policy: if canary misses exceed threshold revert to baseline. we also support pre-warming by replaying common prefixes to the new model so you don't pay big cold-start.
[09:38] Jordan: curious about storage backing — you mentioned nvme, what about persistent cache across restarts?
[09:44] Priya: the NVMe layer stores serialized KV blobs encrypted at rest; on restart we stream hot keys back into memory. persistence reduces cold-start pain especially for on-prem. but for multi-tenant hosted with eviction patterns we still rely mainly on in-memory LRU for perf.
[10:00] Maya: any privacy concerns with storing prefix snippets even redacted?
[10:04] Alex: for strict privacy mode we don't store the snippets, only hashes, and use ephemeral keys. some customers opt for that, but it makes debugging harder. we'll include both options in the security doc.
[10:16] Priya: quick demo note — when we run the benchmark we'll run with instrumentation that outputs CSV with per-route: total requests, cache hits, hit_rate, p50/p95 latency, tokens_saved, and memory used. we'll include a small sample dashboard.
[10:29] Jordan: perfect. a few operational Qs — does cache growth trigger autoscale of GPU pools?
[10:34] Priya: autoscaling is driven by queueing and request latency; cache misses increase GPU load, so indirectly yes. we also expose a metric for cache memory where you can set alerts and autoscale worker nodes if needed.
[10:45] Sam: we care about multi-tenant density — if we do tenant-instance per team, how many tenants per GPU is typical?
[10:52] Priya: depends on model size and request patterns; for 13B models you'd want fewer tenants per GPU, for 7B more. with caching you can increase density because repeated prefixes reduce compute per request. we'll model this in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[11:06] Jordan: any security certifications for hosted?
[11:09] Alex: yes, SOC 2 Type II, and we support SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, and per-tenant KMS. we'll share the SOC2 report and our VPC playbook.
[11:19] Maya: one last deep technical — in the runtime, when resuming from KV cache, how do you handle KV cache alignment for variable-length inputs?
[11:26] Priya: our KV caches are bucketed by sequence-length windows and we store token-offset metadata. when a cached prefix is reused for a longer continuation we replay only the remaining layers. if length mismatch is severe we recompute from scratch. there is a small alignment overhead but it's much cheaper than full recompute.
[11:47] Jordan: thanks. let's recap next steps.
[11:50] Alex: recap: Redwood to run benchmarks with your prompts, Priya to prototype tenant-isolation config, Redwood to send security docs and sample dashboards, Zenith to provide prompts and confirm VPC windows. Pilot kickoff in early September.
[12:03] Jordan: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[12:05] Alex: thanks, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and calendar invite.
[12:08] Priya: thanks all.
